source: Bellemare et al. (2016) Unifying count-based exploration and intrinsic motivation
finding: Core idea: a pseudo-count N^(x) is derived from any density model rho. rho_n(x) is the probability of x before seeing it, rho'_n(x) the 'recoding probability' after one more sighting of x. Pseudo-count solves N^ = rho(1-rho')/(rho'-rho), so one more sighting of x raises it by one.
numbers: Eq. 1-2 in the paper. N^ is zero if rho(x)=0 and infinite if rho'=rho.
limits: Applies only if the density model is learning-positive (rho' >= rho); deep nets can overshoot.
agent_relevance: S3 history of directions: a visit count that generalises across similar states, not just exact repeats.
quote: best thought of as "function approximation for exploration"

source: Bellemare et al. (2016) Unifying count-based exploration and intrinsic motivation
finding: Freeway sanity check: pseudo-counts from a pixel CTS density model act like counts. Near zero on the first road crossing, credible size, ordered by true frequency, linear in real counts on average, robust to a stop-go policy (250,000 frames waiting, then 250,000 frames UP).
numbers: By the end the start position was visited about 140,000 times and the top of the screen 1285 times, yet pseudo-counts were only a fraction of real counts and their ratio differed from the real ratio.
limits: One game, one simple density model (pixel-level CTS, no temporal terms); 10,000-frame averages.
agent_relevance: Counts for 'directions tried' can be approximate and still rank novelty correctly; do not expect exact tallies.

source: Bellemare et al. (2016) Unifying count-based exploration and intrinsic motivation
finding: Theory link: prediction gain PG_n(x) = log rho'_n(x) - log rho_n(x). Pseudo-count and PG are tied: N^ is about (e^PG - 1)^-1. Theorem 1: information gain IG <= PG <= N^^-1, and PG <= N^^-1/2.
numbers: So a bonus of order N^^-1/2 is a safe stand-in for information-gain curiosity. Bonus used in the experiments: R+ = beta (N^ + 0.01)^-1/2.
limits: Theorem holds for mixture (Bayesian) density models; for deep models the link is approximate.
agent_relevance: Unifies count novelty and curiosity/surprise in one number: both are the same quantity under a learning-positive model.

source: Bellemare et al. (2016) Unifying count-based exploration and intrinsic motivation
finding: Why counts beat plain information-gain bonuses in theory: citing Kolter and Ng (2009), no bonus upper-bounded by a 1/N-type decay can guarantee PAC-MDP optimality, so prediction-gain bonuses explore too little compared with pseudo-count bonuses. Pseudo-counts need no forward (transition) model.
numbers: Paper's argument is tabular: Theorem 1 plus the Kolter and Ng result.
limits: Theory is tabular; deep-RL guarantees are not proven. The paper only says it is 'confident' they could be.
agent_relevance: Supports a decaying 1/sqrt(count) bonus on directions rather than a flat novelty flag.

source: Bellemare et al. (2016) Unifying count-based exploration and intrinsic motivation
finding: Hard Atari results (Double DQN with mixed Monte Carlo return, beta=0.05, 5 trials). In Montezuma's Revenge the agent consistently navigated 15 of 24 rooms of level 1 within 50M frames; one run reached 6,600 points by 100M frames. Most earlier agents scored near zero. Large gains also in Venture.
numbers: Optimistic initialisation (Machado et al. 2015) helped only Freeway and otherwise matched DQN. Five 'hard' games: Montezuma, Freeway, Venture, H.E.R.O., Private Eye.
limits: Only 5 trials; beta from a coarse sweep; the mixed Monte Carlo change in the base agent was later shown to matter a lot.
agent_relevance: A count bonus can turn a stuck searcher into one that systematically covers new rooms (new solution regions).

source: Bellemare et al. (2016) Unifying count-based exploration and intrinsic motivation
finding: Actor-critic test on all 60 Atari games: A3C failed to beat 1.5x random on 15 games; A3C+ (with the count bonus) failed on 10 (8 of them also failed by DQN). A3C+ had slightly higher median and clearly beat A3C on at least a quarter of games.
numbers: Scores normalised so 0 and 1 are the min and max of random and A3C end-of-training scores.
limits: Median gain is small; later benchmarks (Taiga) found bonuses can hurt on easy games.
agent_relevance: Bonus helps most where default exploration is weak; gains are concentrated, not uniform.

source: Ostrovski et al. (2017) Count-based exploration with neural density models
finding: Swapped the CTS density model for a PixelCNN. DQN-PixelCNN beat DQN-CTS in 52 of 57 Atari games by max score and 51 by AUC, and set the state of the art on Montezuma's Revenge, Private Eye and Venture.
numbers: Pseudo-count scale c=0.1 with PG decay c*n^-1/2, learning rate 0.001; robust across 1-2 orders of magnitude of c. PG thresholded at 0 because deep models can give negative gain.
limits: Needed a hand-made decay of prediction gain; the raw online PixelCNN PG does not decay properly.
agent_relevance: A better density model gives a better novelty signal, but the signal is still just a count.

source: Ostrovski et al. (2017) Count-based exploration with neural density models
finding: Surprise finding: the mixed Monte Carlo (MMC) return alone explains most of the gain on some games. MMC and the PixelCNN bonus are additive on others, and on some the bonus hurts. Credit assignment was a confound in the 2016 result.
numbers: Seen in Figure 11 and Section 6 of the paper (named games are in the figure).
limits: Per-game numbers only in plots; I did not tabulate them.
agent_relevance: Do not credit a count bonus for what better value propagation (carrying credit back along the path) does.
quote: a powerful facilitator of exploration in the sparsest of settings

source: Ostrovski et al. (2017) Count-based exploration with neural density models
finding: Reactor (multi-step Retrace agent) with PixelCNN bonus (schedule 0.1 n^-1/2) improved sample efficiency (AUC) over plain Reactor in about 50 of 57 games. Retrace's caution slows the spread of exploration reward.
numbers: The 7 sparse-reward hard games gained most; the 40 easy-exploration games gained least (Figure 8 groups).
limits: Gains shown as AUC percentages in a figure only.
agent_relevance: Bonus pays off mostly on sparse-reward subsets; benchmark by group.

source: Ostrovski et al. (2017) Count-based exploration with neural density models
finding: PixelCNN prediction gain never fully vanishes (non-decaying step-size), so the agent stays mildly surprised by big changes, such as entering a new room. These persistent bonuses act as milestones the agent returns to; it repeatedly revisited the torch room just to 'take in the sights'.
numbers: Intrinsic reward trace, Figure 10, Montezuma's Revenge.
limits: Anecdote from one episode; also a side effect: revisiting for bonus without task value.
agent_relevance: A novelty bonus that keeps paying can trap the agent in loops.

source: Tang et al. (2017) #Exploration: a study of count-based exploration for deep RL
finding: SimHash: map states to k-bit codes with a fixed random projection sgn(A g(s)), count visits per code, bonus beta/sqrt(n(code)). With TRPO, pixel-SimHash gave Freeway 31.6 vs 16.5 baseline, Frostbite 4683 vs 2869, Venture 616 vs 121, Montezuma 238 vs 0 (50M steps).
numbers: Atari settings: k=256 bits, beta=0.01. Also close to VIME on sparse-reward continuous control.
limits: Pixel hashing did not help Gravitar (468 vs 486 baseline). Few seeds; Montezuma still very low.
agent_relevance: A cheap hash of the state description is enough to build a usable visit count; no learned density model needed.
quote: a simple yet powerful baseline for solving MDPs that require considerable exploration

source: Tang et al. (2017) #Exploration: a study of count-based exploration for deep RL
finding: Learned hash: an autoencoder with a sigmoid code layer plus noise gives binary codes, then SimHash on them. TRPO-AE-SimHash reached Freeway 33.5, Frostbite 5214, Solaris 2251 (near the state of the art). Hand-built BASS features did better on Montezuma and Venture.
numbers: Hash granularity k matters; codes must stay consistent as the autoencoder trains. Raw pixel hashing clusters similar states poorly.
limits: TRPO-hash Montezuma scores stay far below pseudo-count DQN.
agent_relevance: What goes into the hash (task-relevant features) decides if the count helps. Define 'same direction' carefully in S3.
quote: leads to much better performance on Gravitar, Montezuma's Revenge and Venture

source: Martin et al. (2017) Count-based exploration in feature space (phi-pseudocount)
finding: phi-pseudocount counts feature values seen, using the same features as the value function. Sarsa-phi-EB with Blob-PROST features scored 2745.4 on Montezuma's Revenge, the second-highest then reported, with half the training frames of DDQN-PC.
numbers: beta=0.05 for most games; Freeway needed 0.035 because many irrelevant features give bonus for traffic. Five trials for Montezuma and Venture, two for the rest.
limits: Sensitive to the bonus weight when many features are task-irrelevant (Freeway: agent stands still and farms bonus).
agent_relevance: Measure novelty over task-relevant features only, or the bonus rewards noise.

source: Machado et al. (2018) Count-based exploration with the successor representation
finding: The norm of the successor representation acts as an implicit visit count (substochastic SR). Bonus 1/||SR|| added to Sarsa. Tabular results (in millions of reward): RiverSwim E3 3.0, R-MAX 3.0, MBIE 3.3, ESSR 3.1; SixArms E3 1.8, R-MAX 2.8, MBIE 9.3, ESSR 7.3.
numbers: ESSR averages over 100 runs; baseline numbers taken from Strehl and Littman (2008) histograms.
limits: Below MBIE on SixArms; Atari claim is state-of-the-art only in a low-sample regime.
agent_relevance: Counts can be learned from transition structure (what leads where), not only from state identity.

source: Pathak et al. (2017) Curiosity-driven exploration by self-supervised prediction
finding: Intrinsic Curiosity Module (ICM): reward is forward-model error in a feature space learned by an inverse-dynamics model, so features ignore what the agent cannot control. VizDoom very sparse reward: ICM + A3C reached the perfect score in 66% of random runs; plain A3C and pixel-based ICM never succeeded.
numbers: Distractor test: 40% of the screen replaced by white noise; ICM stayed robust, ICM-pixels failed. No-reward Mario: crosses over 30% of level 1.
limits: Mario progress stops at a pit about 38% along the level; stochasticity handled only via learned features.
agent_relevance: Prediction-error curiosity needs a feature space that drops uncontrollable noise (the noisy-TV problem).

source: Burda et al. (2019) Exploration by random network distillation
finding: Random network distillation: bonus = error of a trained net predicting a fixed random net's output on the observation. With no game score at all, the agent finds more than half the rooms in Montezuma's Revenge. With two value heads and mixed episodic/non-episodic returns the best agent often finds 22 of 24 rooms and sometimes passes level 1.
numbers: Table 1 final mean: Montezuma RND 8,152 vs PPO 2,497, dynamics-error bonus 400, previous SOTA 3,700, average human 4,753.
limits: RND is deterministic so it avoids noisy-TV by design, but fails on Pitfall! (RND -3) and equals PPO on Solaris.
agent_relevance: Cheap novelty from a random target avoids noisy-TV; a non-episodic intrinsic stream explores more than an episodic one.
quote: a mean return of about 2,500 can be reliably achieved without special exploration methods

source: Burda et al. (2019) Exploration by random network distillation
finding: Other games with RND: Private Eye 8,666 vs dynamics bonus 105 (human 69,571); Venture 1,859 vs dynamics bonus 0 (human 1,188); Gravitar 3,906 vs PPO 3,426 vs dynamics 3,371 (human 3,351).
numbers: Non-episodic intrinsic stream beat episodic; gamma_I 0.999 explored more rooms than 0.99, one run reached 21 rooms with no extrinsic reward.
limits: Gravitar: RND did not consistently beat PPO. Two value heads gave no gain over one in the purely episodic case.
agent_relevance: Keep the novelty reward in its own stream and do not end it when one attempt ends.

source: Burda et al. (2019) Exploration by random network distillation
finding: Failure mode seen: once the RND agent has all reachable extrinsic rewards it keeps dying near skulls or moving between rooms to harvest the bonus ('dancing with skulls'). The authors tie it to the noisy-TV / aleatoric uncertainty problem.
numbers: Seen in Venture, Pitfall and Gravitar behaviour at convergence (Section 3.7).
limits: Qualitative, no measured rate.
agent_relevance: A novelty bonus must fade or be gated after the goal is reached, or the agent farms it.

source: Taiga et al. (2020) Benchmarking bonus-based exploration methods on the ALE
finding: Fair re-test: Rainbow agent fixed, 200M frames, all bonuses tuned on Montezuma. Epsilon-greedy does poorly there, but CTS pseudo-count, PixelCNN, ICM, RND and NoisyNets all reliably reach 2,500 points and often more; CTS pseudo-count reaches about 5,000 within 200M frames.
numbers: 5 random seeds per method; bonuses tuned on Montezuma only. Rainbow base is stronger than the DQN used in the originals, so scores rose over the originals.
limits: Their RND uses only the bonus equation, not the other RND tricks.
agent_relevance: A strong base agent plus plain exploration can already match fancy bonuses; ablate the base first.

source: Taiga et al. (2020) Benchmarking bonus-based exploration methods on the ALE
finding: Failed generalisation: Montezuma performance does not correlate with performance on other hard-exploration games; no visible difference between epsilon-greedy and the bonus methods there; epsilon-greedy even beat the others by a wide margin on Gravitar. Bonus methods may hurt on easy-exploration games.
numbers: Games from the Bellemare 2016 hard-exploration set, with bonuses tuned for Montezuma only.
limits: Authors say those games were 'hard' only for weak DQN epsilon-greedy agents; progress may come from credit assignment, not the bonus.
agent_relevance: Counts are no free lunch: test them on tasks other than the one they were tuned on.
quote: these conclusions must be revisited with stronger base agents

source: Burda et al. (2019) Large-scale study of curiosity-driven learning
finding: First large study of curiosity only (no extrinsic reward) across 54 environments. Random features are enough for many game benchmarks; learned (inverse-dynamics) features generalise better to new Mario levels. Adding a noisy TV to a Unity maze drastically slows learning for both inverse-dynamics and random-feature curiosity, though agents sometimes converge if run long.
numbers: 54 environments including Atari; TV test in Figure 6.
limits: Studies dynamics-prediction curiosity, not counts; TV result is qualitative.
agent_relevance: Same warning for any novelty drive: a random source in the context attracts it.
quote: presence of the TV drastically slows down learning

source: Badia et al. (2020) Never Give Up: learning directed exploration strategies
finding: Combines in-episode novelty (k-nearest-neighbour similarity to a memory of controllable-state embeddings) with a lifelong RND multiplier. Doubles the base agent on all hard-exploration Atari games, median human-normalised score 1344.0% over 57 games, first non-zero Pitfall! (mean 8,400) without demonstrations.
numbers: In their ablation, R2D2 and R2D2+RND reach super-human only on Montezuma among the hard games; RND alone hurt Pitfall!. 35 billion frames per agent.
limits: Very heavy compute; Montezuma stability needed a clipped lifelong factor.
agent_relevance: Two timescales of count: novelty inside one attempt times novelty across attempts. Maps to S3 within a run vs across runs.
quote: first algorithm to achieve non-zero rewards

source: Ecoffet et al. (2019) Go-Explore: a new approach for hard-exploration problems
finding: Go-Explore (abstract read) keeps an archive of visited states, returns to a promising state without exploring, then explores from it. Montezuma: over 43,000 points with no domain knowledge (almost 4x previous SOTA); mean over 650,000 with human knowledge; max 18 million. First algorithm above zero on Pitfall (with domain knowledge).
numbers: Phase 1 solves simulated environments by any means, including introducing determinism; then robustified by imitation learning.
limits: Only the abstract and first page were read; the 2021 Nature paper supersedes this version.
agent_relevance: Argues S3 should be an archive plus return-to-state, not just a bonus. Link to subfield 08 Go-Explore.
quote: remember states that have previously been visited

source: Strehl and Littman (2008) An analysis of model-based interval estimation for Markov decision processes
finding: The tabular ancestor: MBIE-EB adds a bonus beta/sqrt(N(s,a)) to estimated reward and proves PAC-MDP sample bounds. Bellemare's bonus (N^+0.01)^-1/2 is this rule with a pseudo-count. Known here only through Machado 2018 and Bellemare 2016.
numbers: Not opened.
limits: Tabular finite MDPs only.
agent_relevance: Origin of the 1/sqrt(count) rule.

source: Kolter and Ng (2009) Near-Bayesian exploration in polynomial time
finding: Cited by Bellemare 2016 for the result that a bonus decaying too fast (upper-bounded by a 1/N-type rate) cannot guarantee PAC-MDP optimality. Used to argue information-gain bonuses explore too little.
numbers: Not opened; description from Bellemare 2016 section 4.
limits: Tabular analysis.
agent_relevance: Sets how fast an exploration bonus may decay.
